questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Select a tool for a stated art task and explain how to care for it.
questions.prompt: A pupil using watercolour needs to cover a wide background evenly. Which tool is best suited to that part of the work?
questions.explanation: A broad flat brush can cover a larger area with fewer strokes. A pointed brush is more useful for narrow details.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Select a tool for a stated art task and explain how to care for it.
questions.prompt: Demonstrate how you would care for a brush just used with watercolour. Use the teacher’s designated water container and return the brush to the drying area.
questions.answer: Rinse the brush until visible colour is removed, gently blot excess water, reshape the bristles and lay the brush flat in the designated drying area.
questions.explanation: Removing pigment keeps it from drying in the brush. Blotting and laying the brush flat help protect its shape.

markingGuide.description: Uses the designated container and removes visible paint.
Blots and reshapes the bristles without pulling them.
Places the brush appropriately in the designated area.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Explain how line direction or spacing can represent light, shade and surface texture.
questions.prompt: A pupil shades the same pencil drawing with parallel lines. Which change makes one area appear darker while retaining this technique?
questions.explanation: Closer parallel strokes cover more of the paper, making the area read as a darker tone.
options: Erase every line from that area.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Explain how line direction or spacing can represent light, shade and surface texture.
questions.prompt: Sketch a smooth bottle and a rough woven basket on one sheet. Add two kinds of marks that help the viewer distinguish the surfaces. Label each mark and explain its purpose.
questions.answer: The bottle uses smooth gradual shading with a light highlight. The basket uses short crossing strokes in repeated bands to suggest interwoven strips.
questions.explanation: Contrasting mark patterns make the material differences visible. The marks should match what the pupil observes or intends to suggest.

markingGuide.description: Uses suitable marks for the smooth surface.
Uses distinct marks for the woven surface.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Identify the drawing type from the main subject and arrangement.
questions.prompt: A pupil arranges a cup, a closed book and an orange on a table and draws them from one viewing position. Which type of drawing is this?
questions.explanation: A still life depicts arranged objects. The cup, book and orange are the subjects of the composition.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.subtopic: Drawing a still life from observation
questions.learningObjective: Draw an arrangement of objects using relative size, overlap and a consistent light direction.
questions.prompt: Place a cup partly in front of a closed book. Draw the arrangement from your seat. Show which object is closer and use one light direction to shade the scene.
questions.answer: A successful drawing shows the cup overlapping the book, keeps their relative sizes close to the observed arrangement and places darker tones and cast shadow consistently with the light source.
questions.explanation: Overlap helps show depth. Consistent shading makes the volume and position of the objects easier to read.

markingGuide.description: Draws both observed objects with recognisable shapes.
Shows the cup overlapping the book.
Uses shading consistent with one light direction.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Draw a landscape that distinguishes foreground and distance through placement, relative size or detail.
questions.prompt: From a teacher-approved view of the school grounds, draw a landscape with one near feature and one distant feature. Use placement and at least one other visual clue to make the depth clear.
questions.answer: For example, draw a large, detailed tree near the lower edge and a smaller, simpler school building farther up the page. The near feature may overlap part of the distant view if that is what you observe.
questions.explanation: Position and relative detail or size can suggest depth. The example allows other views and layouts that communicate the same relationship.

markingGuide.description: Places a near and a distant feature coherently.
Uses a second cue such as overlap, scale or detail to show depth.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Identify how modelling can build volume by shaping and adding material.
questions.prompt: To make a clay animal, a pupil forms a body and joins separate clay pieces for the legs. Which feature makes this an example of modelling?
questions.answer: The pupil shapes and adds soft material to build a form.
questions.explanation: Joining and shaping soft clay builds a three-dimensional form.
options: The pupil shapes and adds soft material to build a form.
The pupil cuts a shape out of a block of wood.
The pupil paints a flat shape on paper.
The pupil folds a sheet into a two-dimensional pattern.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Model a small clay vessel with a cavity, stable base and controlled wall shape.
questions.prompt: Using teacher-provided modelling clay, shape a small pinch pot for display. Make a cavity, keep the wall fairly even and check that the base rests steadily on a flat board.
questions.answer: A successful pot has a clear cavity, continuous walls without conspicuous thin spots and a broad enough base to stand without rocking.
questions.explanation: The cavity makes the form recognisable as a vessel. Wall control and a steady base are visible signs of successful modelling.

markingGuide.description: Forms a recognisable vessel with a cavity.
Keeps the walls continuous and reasonably even.
Produces a base that stands steadily.
Finishes the rim without conspicuous tears or loose pieces.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a tied area can resist dye and form a lighter mark.
questions.prompt: A cloth is tied tightly around a small gathered section before dyeing. When the tie is removed, why might part of that section appear lighter?
questions.answer: The tight tie limits how much dye reaches that part.
questions.explanation: The tie acts as a resist by limiting dye penetration where the cloth is compressed.
options: The tied cloth becomes a different fibre.
The tight tie limits how much dye reaches that part.
The tie makes the whole cloth absorb dye at the same rate.
The knot makes the dye lighter everywhere.
